newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge defectors say prince's men plotted coup.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge defectors say prince's men plotted coup.

text.p: Four defectors from Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said on Tuesday that First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's top military commander infiltrated Khmer Rouge defectors into the capital for a planned coup.

The defectors said Ranariddh's top commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, had plans to bring 10,000 Khmer Rouge fighters to Phnom Penh to attack rival Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's forces and take power.

"Nhiek Bun Chhay wanted to bring 10,000 Khmer Rouge to Phnom Penh and 1,600 to Kompong Cham in order to fight and take power from Second Prime Minister Hun Sen," one of the defectors, Phon Peap, told a news conference organised by the ministry of information.
Kompong Cham is a province just to the north of Phnom Penh.
"They brought Khmer Rouge to Phnom Penh in order to fight with the Cambodian People's Party," Phon Peap said, referring to Hun Sen's political party.
Ranariddh was overthrown on July 6 after two days of fighting in the capital initiated by Hun Sen's forces.
Hun Sen has gone to great lengths to justify his action against Ranriddh's forces which sparked the fighting and led to the loss of at least 58 lives and left up to 200 wounded.
Most of the casualties were civilians caught in crossfire as the two sides battled in the city centre and its outskirts.

Last week the foreign ministry published a White Paper in English giving details of Ranariddh's "strategy of provocation" including his attempts to strengthen his forces with Khmer Rouge defectors and arm them with smuggled weapons.

Hun Sen denied staging a coup against Ranariddh. He said he had to take action against Ranariddh's military commanders because they were bringing "illegal forces" and weapons into Phnom Penh to bolster the prince's troop strength.
Ranariddh denied his commanders were smuggling Khmer Rouge defectors into the city.
The four told the news conference that when they defected from the Khmer Rouge they thought they were joining the government army but they soon found they were actually in units loyal to Ranariddh.

Three of the four said they had left Ranariddh's side and switched to Hun Sen's side before the July 5-6 fighting, while the fourth, a 16-year-old, said he had escaped from a base under Nhiek Bun Chhay's control during the fighting.
Hun Sen said Ranariddh was a traitor and should be prosecuted for his alleged crimes, including holding illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge and arms smuggling.
The second prime minister said on Monday that a Cambodian court should prepare an international warrant for Ranariddh's arrest.
The Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, responsible for the death of a million people during their 1975-79 rule, has been hit by a wave of defections in recent years.
Both prime ministers tried to lure defecting guerrillas to their side as a power-sharing row between them worsened and their unwieldly coalition government came under increasing strain.

Ranariddh won a U.N.-supervised election in 1993 but agreed to a coalition with Hun Sen after the leader of the former government objected to the poll result and the country faced divison along factional lines.
